notes: Chilean Cabernet Sauvignon is easy drinking, with soft tannins and flavors of mint, blackcurrant, olive and smoke.
Cool Andes nights keep acidity high alongside ripe fruit from long, sunny days.
Chilean Sauvignon Blanc is noticeably less acidic than New Zealand's, closer to the French style.
Chilean Malbec is more tannic than Argentina's and is used mostly in Bordeaux-style blends.
Aconcagua wines are noted for ripe fruit but a closed, tight structure that needs time in bottle.

Casablanca is known for fresh, complex Sauvignon Blanc.
Colchagua is best known for full bodied Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère and Syrah.
Its warmth ripens grapes fully, giving rich fruit that can seem sweet.
Curicó is a reliable workhorse region, and its warmth gives rich, very ripe fruit flavors.
Maipo Cabernet Sauvignon is marked by pervasive blackcurrant fruit and an earthy, dusty note.
Maule is best known for powerful Cabernet Sauvignon and aromatic, spicy Carmenère.
Old Carignan vines give soft, earthy reds with rich plum and black fruit.
Newer plantings of Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Carmenère show bright acidity and juicy fruit.
Limarí is best known for Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay, and also makes Syrah and Pinot Noir.
Morning fog from the Pacific and mineral-rich soils give fresh wines with a distinct mineral edge.
The Bío-Bío Valley has become known for crisp, aromatic wines.
The Andes and Coastal Range trap warm, dry air here, while cool Andes nights keep acidity high alongside ripe fruit.
Malbec grown across the Central Valley is more tannic than Argentina's and goes mostly into Bordeaux-style blends.
Elqui is arid, with clear skies, and Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc lead.
In its cool climate, Syrah becomes spicy and complex.
In the Elqui Valley, Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc lead, and the cool climate makes Syrah spicy and complex.
The Limarí Valley's limestone soils and sea breezes give Chardonnay an attractive minerality.
Limarí Syrah is also well regarded.
Cachapoal is known for reds, mainly Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, about 80% of its output.
Cool-climate grapes grow in high vineyards in the Andes foothills, and warmer ones near Lake Rapel.
Bright sun, Andes breezes and cool nights give consistent, high-quality Cabernet Sauvignon.
